questions.question_text:
The government has £2 billion to spend. It is deciding whether to spend it on building a new hospital or on new roads.

Using this example, explain what is meant by opportunity cost and why it arises.

points: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
It arises because resources are scarce / limited while wants are unlimited, so choices have to be made
Applied: if the government builds the hospital, the opportunity cost is the roads (or the benefits of the roads) it can no longer build
Applied: the £2 billion can only be spent once, so spending it on one means sacrificing the other
scheme.guidance: Two marks for knowledge and two for applying it to the hospital and roads. 'The cost of something' alone does not define opportunity cost.

questions.question_text:
A poor harvest in Brazil has reduced the world supply of coffee beans. At the same time, coffee has become more popular in China.

Analyse the likely effects of these two changes on the equilibrium price and quantity of coffee beans. You may describe a supply and demand diagram in words.

levels.descriptor: Clear chains of reasoning for both changes, correctly identifying the effect on price and a reasoned conclusion about quantity (which depends on the relative size of the shifts).
Correct analysis of one change, or both changes with limited development.
Simple statements, e.g. price will rise, with little explanation.

indicative: The poor harvest shifts the supply curve to the left (decrease in supply)
The decrease in supply causes excess demand at the old price, so the price rises and quantity falls
Greater popularity in China shifts the demand curve to the right (increase in demand)
The increase in demand causes excess demand, so the price rises and quantity rises
Both changes push the price up, so the equilibrium price will definitely rise
The effect on quantity is uncertain: it depends on whether the supply shift or the demand shift is bigger
Price acts as a rationing signal: higher price reduces quantity demanded and encourages other producers to supply
scheme.guidance: Shifts must be distinguished from movements along a curve for Level 3. Credit a clearly described diagram.

questions.question_text:
A cinema raises the price of a ticket from £8.00 to £10.00. The number of tickets sold each week falls from 2000 to 1700.

Calculate the price elasticity of demand (PED) for cinema tickets, and state whether demand is price elastic or price inelastic. Show your working.

points: Percentage change in quantity demanded = (1700 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = −15%
Percentage change in price = (10 − 8) ÷ 8 × 100 = +25%
Demand is price inelastic because the PED is less than 1 (ignoring the sign)
scheme.guidance: Accept 0.6 without the minus sign. Allow error carried forward for the elastic/inelastic judgement. This question asks for working. A correct final answer with no working scores only the mark(s) for the answer itself, not the method marks. Award each method mark when that step is shown. If the working has a slip (e.g. a wrong number copied) but the final answer is correct, withhold only the mark(s) for the step that is wrong.

questions.question_text:
A small bakery is growing into a large bakery chain with shops across the country.

Explain two economies of scale the bakery chain might benefit from as it grows.

points: Purchasing / bulk-buying economies: buying flour and ingredients in large quantities at a lower price per unit
Technical economies: using larger, more efficient ovens or machinery, so the cost per loaf falls
Financial economies: larger firms can borrow more cheaply / at lower interest rates
Marketing economies: the cost of advertising is spread over more shops and output
Managerial economies: hiring specialist managers, increasing efficiency
Each economy explained as lowering the average cost (cost per unit)
scheme.guidance: Max 4: up to 2 marks for each economy, one for identifying it and one for explaining how it lowers average cost in the bakery's context.

questions.question_text:
Two companies supply most of the UK's train tickets on a popular route, after one bought the other's rival.

Evaluate whether a monopoly is always bad for consumers.

levels.descriptor: Good knowledge applied well; developed chains of reasoning showing both costs and benefits of monopoly; a supported judgement that answers 'always'.
Reasonable knowledge with some analysis of costs and benefits; evaluation is limited or one-sided.
Limited knowledge with simple points; little or no analysis or evaluation.

indicative: A monopoly is a single seller with a large share of the market (legal definition 25%+)
Monopolies may charge higher prices because consumers have no alternative
Less choice and less incentive to improve quality or customer service
Possible inefficiency because there is no competitive pressure to keep costs down
But monopolies can gain economies of scale, which could lower prices
Supernormal profits may be invested in research and development and innovation
Natural monopolies (e.g. rail track, water) may be more efficient with one firm
Government regulation (e.g. the Competition and Markets Authority, price caps) can protect consumers
Judgement: depends on regulation, barriers to entry and how the firm uses its profits, so not always bad
scheme.guidance: Level 3 requires a justified conclusion that addresses 'always'.

questions.question_text:
A factory releases smoke that pollutes the air in a nearby town.

Explain why this is an example of market failure.

points: This is a negative externality: a cost to a third party not involved in the transaction
The town's residents suffer costs such as health problems or cleaning costs that the factory doesn't pay for
The factory doesn't take the external cost into account, so the price of its product is too low
So too much of the product is produced / consumed: resources are misallocated, which is market failure
scheme.guidance: The final mark needs the idea of overproduction or misallocation of resources.

questions.subtopic: Interest rates, saving, borrowing, spending, investment
questions.question_text: Explain how a rise in interest rates is likely to affect households' spending and saving.

points: Saving becomes more attractive because savers earn more interest
So households save more and spend less
Borrowing becomes more expensive (e.g. loans, credit cards), so households borrow less to spend
Mortgage repayments rise for households with variable-rate mortgages, leaving less disposable income to spend
scheme.guidance: Max 4. Each mark needs a link between the interest rate and the behaviour, not just a statement.

questions.question_text:
UK inflation rose above 10% in 2022.

Explain the possible effects of high inflation on consumers and on businesses.

levels.descriptor: Developed chains of reasoning explaining effects on both consumers and businesses.
Some explained effects on consumers or businesses, or both with limited development.
Simple statements, e.g. prices go up, with little explanation.

indicative: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured by the CPI
Consumers' real incomes fall if wages rise more slowly than prices, so they can buy less
People on fixed incomes, e.g. some pensioners, are hit hardest
The real value of savings falls if inflation is higher than the interest rate
Businesses face higher costs of raw materials, energy and wages, reducing profit
Uncertainty makes businesses less likely to invest
UK exports become less price competitive abroad
Borrowers may gain because the real value of debt falls
scheme.guidance: Level 3 needs both consumers and businesses.

questions.question_text:
The UK economy is in a recession and unemployment is rising.

Evaluate whether the government should increase its spending to reduce unemployment.

levels.descriptor: Good knowledge applied well; developed chains of reasoning on how spending affects unemployment and its drawbacks; a supported judgement.
Reasonable knowledge with some analysis; evaluation limited or one-sided.
Limited knowledge with simple points; little analysis or evaluation.

indicative: Increasing government spending is expansionary fiscal policy
Spending on infrastructure, e.g. building projects, creates jobs directly
It increases total demand in the economy, so firms need more workers (derived demand for labour)
There may be a multiplier effect as newly employed workers spend their incomes
But it increases the budget deficit and national debt, which must be repaid with interest or higher taxes later
It may take time for projects to start (time lags)
It could cause inflation if the economy is near full capacity
It may not help structural unemployment if the jobs created don't match workers' skills
Alternatives: cut interest rates (monetary policy), training schemes (supply-side), tax cuts
Judgement: depends on the type of unemployment, size of existing debt and how the money is spent

questions.question_text:
The value of the pound has fallen from £1 = $1.40 to £1 = $1.20.

Analyse how this fall in the value of the pound might affect UK exporters and UK consumers.

levels.descriptor: Developed chains of reasoning covering both exporters and consumers, using the exchange rate context.
Some analysis of effects on exporters or consumers, or both with limited development.

indicative: The pound has depreciated: each pound buys fewer dollars
UK exports become cheaper in dollars, e.g. a £100 item falls from $140 to $120
So demand for UK exports rises, increasing exporters' revenue and possibly jobs
Imports become more expensive in pounds, e.g. a $120 item rises from about £86 to £100
UK consumers pay more for imported goods, e.g. holidays abroad, fuel and electronics, reducing real incomes
Exporters that use imported raw materials face higher costs
Higher import prices can cause inflation
scheme.guidance: Credit worked numerical examples as application.
